Electrical Safety: Shock, Leakage, Grounding, and GFCI

Unit 3: Public Safety in the Healthcare Facility. Lesson 15 of 60 in CBET Academy.

Patients are more vulnerable to electricity than anyone else in the building: they are wet, sedated, and sometimes wired directly to the heart. Electrical safety is the biomed's core duty.

What current does to the body

For 60 Hz current through the body from hand to hand:

  • About 1 mA: the threshold of perception, a tingle.
  • 5 mA: the accepted maximum harmless current.
  • 10 to 20 mA: the let-go threshold; muscles clamp and the person cannot release the conductor.
  • Around 50 mA: pain, fainting, possible respiratory arrest.
  • 100 to 300 mA: ventricular fibrillation is likely; this is the lethal range.
  • 6 A and above: sustained contraction of the heart, severe burns.

Macroshock and microshock

Macroshock is current entering through the skin. The skin's resistance limits it, and it takes milliamps to hurt. Microshock is current that bypasses the skin and reaches the heart directly through a catheter, pacing wire, or fluid-filled line. There, as little as 10 microamps can trigger fibrillation. That is why patient-connected equipment is held to microamp leakage limits.

Where leakage comes from

Every powered device leaks a little current to its chassis through the capacitance of its power cord, transformer windings, and filters, plus any insulation defect. Normally the ground wire carries that leakage harmlessly away. If the ground opens, the chassis sits at a voltage and the leakage looks for another path, possibly through a patient touching the case and a grounded bed rail.

Grounding

The green wire and the third prong exist to give fault and leakage current a low-resistance path back to the source so a breaker trips or the current is diverted. A broken ground pin, a two-prong adapter, or a damaged cord removes that protection. Ground resistance on patient-care equipment must stay below 0.5 ohm (NFPA 99).

Cord and plug inspection

Check for cracked insulation, bent or missing ground pins, strain relief pulled out, and burned contacts. Replace the cord; never tape it. Hospital-grade plugs and receptacles have a green dot. Extension cords and unapproved power strips are prohibited for patient care equipment; approved relocatable power taps must be rated, secured, and never daisy-chained. Know the power cord color coding when you open a plug or an inlet: US cords run black (or red) for hot, white for neutral, and green or bare for ground; IEC cords use brown for live, blue for neutral, and green-yellow for ground.

GFCI and isolated power

A GFCI trips when about 5 mA more leaves on the hot wire than returns on the neutral, protecting people near water from macroshock; it does nothing against microshock because its threshold is a thousand times too high. Isolated power with a line isolation monitor removes the ground reference entirely so a first fault causes no current flow; the LIM alarms at 5 mA of total hazard current so the fault is found before a second one appears.

Habits that prevent shock

Keep patient-connected leads away from grounded metal. Never plug a patient-connected device into an ungrounded outlet. Report tingles immediately; a tingle is a fault. Test after every repair.

Exam tip: 10 mA let-go, 100 mA fibrillation, 10 microamps microshock. Ground resistance 0.5 ohm. GFCI at 5 mA protects against macroshock, not microshock. An open ground turns leakage into a hazard.
Remember
1 mA feel, 10 mA let-go, 100 mA fibrillate, 10 microamps to the heart is microshock. Leakage rides the ground wire; an open ground makes it a hazard. Ground resistance 0.5 ohm. GFCI 5 mA, LIM 5 mA.
Deeper explanation

Electrical Safety: Shock, Leakage, Grounding, and GFCI, explained slowly

The patient is the weakest circuit in the building

Electrical safety in a hospital is different from a factory for one reason: patients have had their natural defenses removed. They are wet with conductive fluids, their skin has been prepped and punctured, they cannot let go, and some have a wire or a fluid column running straight to the heart. This lesson is the physics of what current does and how the facility keeps it away from them.

What current does, and why

Nerves and muscles fire on electrical pulses. Fifty or sixty hertz is slow enough that each cycle acts as a stimulus, so the effects scale with current:

about 1 mA       perception: tingling; sensory nerves fire
5 mA             maximum harmless: startling but no injury
10 to 20 mA      let-go threshold: forearm muscles clamp the hand around the conductor;
                 the victim cannot release, and exposure continues
about 50 mA      pain, fainting; chest muscles may freeze (respiratory arrest)
100 to 300 mA    ventricular fibrillation: the heart's cells fire chaotically and it stops pumping
6 A and above    the heart clamps in sustained contraction; severe burns; may restart when released

Time matters too: a longer exposure at a lower current does the same damage. And the path matters: hand to hand or hand to foot crosses the chest and the heart; that is the dangerous path.

Macroshock versus microshock

MACROSHOCK   current enters through the SKIN            skin resistance limits it; milliamps to hurt
             ordinary electrocution; a person touching a faulty chassis while grounded
MICROSHOCK   current bypasses the skin and reaches the   no skin resistance; MICROamps can fibrillate
             HEART directly through a catheter, pacing   the threshold usually cited is 10 microamps
             wire, or fluid-filled pressure line

The microshock patient is the reason leakage limits for cardiac-connected equipment are measured in microamps, a thousand times tighter than what protects an ordinary person. A nurse touching a faulty device with one hand and the patient's pacing wire with the other could deliver a lethal microshock and feel nothing herself.

Where leakage comes from

No device is perfectly insulated. Current leaks to the chassis through:

  • capacitance between the power cord conductors and the ground wire,
  • capacitance in transformer windings,
  • the filter capacitors that suppress radio interference,
  • any degraded or wet insulation.

This is normal and small, tens to hundreds of microamps. The ground wire returns it to the panel harmlessly. The danger begins when the ground path is broken.

GOOD:  chassis --leakage--> ground wire --> panel        patient touches chassis: current takes the ground path
BAD:   chassis --leakage--> [open ground pin]            chassis floats at some voltage;
       patient touches chassis and a grounded bed rail:  ALL the leakage goes through the patient

A broken ground does not stop the device working, so nobody notices until the safety test, or the shock.

Grounding and the ground test

The third prong and the green wire give fault current a path of almost no resistance back to the source, so a real fault trips the breaker in milliseconds and leakage is diverted around people. NFPA 99 requires the resistance from the chassis to the plug's ground pin to be no more than 0.5 ohm on patient-care equipment; a worn plug, a corroded internal strap, or a damaged cord raises it.

Cords, plugs, and outlets

Inspect every cord at every PM: cracked insulation, exposed conductors, a strain relief pulled loose, a bent or missing ground pin, scorched blades. Replace, never tape. Hospital-grade plugs and receptacles (green dot) hold tighter and are built for the abuse. Two-prong adapters and extension cords are forbidden for patient-care equipment. Relocatable power taps are allowed only if rated, secured, used within their capacity, and never plugged into one another. Power cord color coding is part of the inspection whenever a plug has been replaced: US cords black (hot), white (neutral), green (ground); IEC cords brown, blue, green-yellow. A cord rewired with hot and neutral swapped passes a continuity check and fails the reversed-polarity leakage test, which is one reason the analyzer runs that condition.

Two protective systems, two different jobs

  • GFCI: watches for current leaving on the hot conductor that does not come back on the neutral. At about 5 mA of difference it opens the circuit. It saves a person touching a faulty device in a wet area. It does nothing for a microshock patient; 5 mA is far above the cardiac threshold.
  • Isolated power with a line isolation monitor: neither conductor is grounded, so the first fault to ground causes no current at all. The LIM measures the insulation and alarms at 5 mA of total hazard current, which means "a first fault exists; find it before a second one turns this into a circuit."

Habits

Report tingles; a tingle is a fault waiting for a wetter victim. Keep patient leads off metal. Never disable a ground to "stop the hum." Test after every repair, because a repair can loosen a ground strap.

How the exam asks it

  • "The current level at which a person cannot release a conductor?" About 10 to 20 mA.
  • "Which condition allows microshock?" A direct conductive path to the heart such as a catheter.
  • "Why is an open ground dangerous even though the device still works?" Leakage current has no safe path and may flow through the patient.
  • "Maximum ground resistance for patient-care equipment?" 0.5 ohm.
  • "Does a GFCI protect a patient with a central line from microshock?" No.

What to memorize

  • 1 mA feel, 10 to 20 mA let-go, 100 mA fibrillate, 6 A clamp. Microshock at 10 microamps to the heart.
  • Leakage is normal; an open ground makes it a hazard. Ground resistance 0.5 ohm.
  • GFCI at 5 mA protects people from macroshock; the LIM alarms at 5 mA hazard current on isolated power.
